meta.titre: Growth of Firms: internal growth, mergers and the types of integration
meta.sous_theme: Internal and external growth, types of integration and economies of scale

sections.contenu_markdown: Imagine a small bakery in Douala with one oven. In time, its owner uses her profits to open a second shop, then buys the flour mill that supplies her, and later joins with another baker in a different town. Each step makes the business bigger, but each step is a different kind of growth. GCE papers regularly ask students to define integration, to classify a merger as horizontal, vertical or conglomerate, and to say why firms want to grow.

items: A firm is a business unit that produces goods or services to earn a profit.
Average cost is total cost divided by the number of units produced.
Production passes through stages, from raw materials to the sale to the consumer.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Ways in which a firm grows
**Internal (organic) growth** is expansion using the firm's own resources: ploughing back profits into new equipment, opening new branches or selling new products. **External growth** is expansion by joining with other firms. In a **merger** two firms agree to combine into one. In a **takeover** one firm buys control of another, usually by buying its shares. The joining of firms is called **integration of firms**.

### Types of integration

| Type | Firms joined | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Horizontal | Same product, same stage of production | Two bakeries |
| Vertical backward | Same product, an earlier stage (towards raw materials or suppliers) | A cement maker buys a limestone quarry |
| Vertical forward | Same product, a later stage (towards the consumer) | A shoe factory buys its own shops |
| Conglomerate | Firms in unrelated businesses | A soap factory joins a bus company |

### Why firms grow
* **Economies of scale**: the average cost of a unit falls as output rises. Internal economies are savings inside one firm (technical, managerial, financial, marketing and risk-bearing). External economies are advantages that all firms in an industry enjoy when the industry grows, such as a pool of trained workers and better transport and supplier firms.
* **Larger market share** and more power over prices.
* **Spreading of risk**: a firm in several businesses is less hurt when one of them does badly (conglomerates).
* **Secure supply** of raw materials or secure outlets (vertical integration).

### Limits to growth
Diseconomies of scale: a firm that becomes too large has difficulty in managing and communicating, so average cost rises. Other limits are a small market, shortage of capital and government laws that control monopolies.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a case describes two firms joining
variantes.contenu_markdown: Ask what each firm makes and where it stands in the chain from raw material to consumer. Same product and same stage: horizontal. Same product but different stages: vertical (backward if towards suppliers, forward if towards customers). Unrelated businesses: conglomerate.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to distinguish the two
variantes.contenu_markdown: A merger is an agreement between firms to form one. A takeover happens when one firm buys control of another, sometimes against the wishes of its managers.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks about the effect of size on cost
variantes.contenu_markdown: Economies of scale lower the average cost as output grows. Diseconomies of scale raise the average cost when the firm becomes too large to manage well.

sections.enonce_markdown:
State the type of integration in each case.
(a) A cement manufacturer buys a company that owns limestone quarries.
(b) A supermarket chain merges with another supermarket chain.
(c) A furniture maker buys a chain of showrooms that sell only its products.
(d) A timber company merges with a chain of hotels.
(e) The two supermarket chains in (b) sell 2,400 million FCFA and 1,600 million FCFA in a market whose total sales are 8,000 million FCFA. Calculate their combined market share after the merger.

etapes.justification: The quarry supplies a raw material of cement and is at an earlier stage.
Both firms sell to consumers and are at the same stage of production.
The showrooms are closer to the consumer than the factory.
The two businesses have nothing to do with each other.
Share is sales divided by total sales, times 100.
After a merger the sales add up.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) Vertical backward. (b) Horizontal. (c) Vertical forward. (d) Conglomerate. (e) The merged firm holds 50% of the market, which gives it more power over price.

items.erreur_markdown: "Horizontal integration is the joining of firms at different stages of production."
items.correction_markdown: Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage of production of the same product.

items.erreur_markdown: "A merger between a bank and a bakery is horizontal because both are businesses."
items.pourquoi_faux: Horizontal integration requires the same kind of product and stage.
items.correction_markdown: A bank and a bakery produce unrelated goods and services, so the merger is conglomerate.

items.erreur_markdown: "A firm can grow only by merging with another firm."
items.pourquoi_faux: Merging is only one way. The firm can also expand on its own.
items.correction_markdown: Internal growth is possible by ploughing back profits, opening new branches or launching new products.

items.erreur_markdown: "The bigger a firm is, the lower its costs will always be."
items.pourquoi_faux: Beyond a certain size, management and communication problems raise costs.
items.correction_markdown: Costs fall through economies of scale up to a point; then diseconomies of scale can raise average cost.

items.erreur_markdown: "External economies of scale are the savings made inside one large firm."
items.pourquoi_faux: Savings inside a firm are internal economies.
items.correction_markdown: External economies are benefits to all firms in an industry because the industry has grown, such as a pool of skilled workers.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain the difference between internal growth and external growth of a firm, giving one example of each.
items.solution_markdown: **Internal growth** is expansion with the firm's own resources, for example ploughing back profits to open a new branch. **External growth** is expansion by joining with other firms, for example a merger with another firm or a takeover.

items.enonce_markdown:
A firm earns a profit of 12 million FCFA in year 1 and 15 million FCFA in year 2. It ploughs back 60% of each year's profit to buy a machine that costs 18 million FCFA.
(a) Calculate the amount ploughed back in each year.
(b) Calculate the total amount available after two years.
(c) Calculate the shortfall that the firm still has to borrow.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Year 1: $0.6 \times 12 =$ **7.2 million FCFA**. Year 2: $0.6 \times 15 =$ **9 million FCFA**.
(b) $7.2 + 9 =$ **16.2 million FCFA**.
(c) $18 - 16.2 =$ **1.8 million FCFA**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Two soap makers merge. Firm X produces 40,000 bars at a total cost of 80 million FCFA. Firm Y produces 60,000 bars at a total cost of 150 million FCFA. After the merger the new firm produces 100,000 bars at a total cost of 190 million FCFA.
(a) Name the type of integration.
(b) Calculate the average cost of X, of Y and of the merged firm.
(c) Calculate the percentage fall in average cost compared with the combined average cost before the merger.
(d) Give one reason why costs may fall and one danger for consumers.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Horizontal integration**, because both make soap at the same stage.
(b) X: $\frac{80\,000\,000}{40\,000} =$ **2,000 FCFA**. Y: $\frac{150\,000\,000}{60\,000} =$ **2,500 FCFA**. Merged firm: $\frac{190\,000\,000}{100\,000} =$ **1,900 FCFA**.
(c) Before the merger: $\frac{230\,000\,000}{100\,000} = 2\,300$ FCFA. The fall is $\frac{2\,300 - 1\,900}{2\,300} \times 100 =$ **17.4%**.
(d) Costs fall through economies of scale, for example bulk buying and one management team. The danger is that with less competition the firm may raise prices.

items_markdown: Internal growth uses the firm's own resources; external growth joins firms by merger or takeover.
Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage; vertical integration joins different stages; conglomerate integration joins unrelated businesses.
Firms grow to enjoy economies of scale, gain market share, spread risk and secure supplies.
Internal economies are inside one firm; external economies come from the growth of the whole industry.
Growth is limited by diseconomies of scale, a small market, shortage of capital and government control of monopolies.
